rows.speaker: سالم بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Salim reports that Marwan sought Hafsa’s source sheets; after her death Ibn Umar sent them, and Marwan destroyed them to prevent later doubts because their contents were preserved in the codex; Ibn Kathir grades the chain sound.
rows.anchor: أخبرني سالم بن عبد الله: أن مروان كان يرسل إلى حفصة يسألها الصحف

rows.speaker: الزهري عن خارجة عن أبيه
rows.claim: A report through al-Zuhri, Kharija, and his father says an al-Ahzab verse was attached to its surah; Ibn Kathir says this report is wrongly placed after Uthman’s compilation.
rows.anchor: ما رواه الزهري (3) عن خارجة عن أبيه في شأن آية الأحزاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir holds that attaching the al-Ahzab verse occurred during Abu Bakr’s collection, citing another al-Zuhri report via Ubayy ibn al-Sabbaq from Zayd ibn Thabit; Uthmani copies do not place it in a margin.
rows.anchor: هذا كان حال جمع الصديق الصحف كما جاء مصرحا به في غير هذه الرواية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir praises Abu Bakr and Umar’s collection to preserve the Qur’an and Uthman’s unification of the readings in one codex, following the final presentation to Gabriel.
rows.anchor: فهذه الأفعال (6) من أكبر القربات التي بادر إليها الأئمة الراشدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet reviewed the Qur’an with Gabriel twice in his final Ramadan; Ibn Kathir links this to the Prophet telling Fatima during his illness that he thought his death was near, a report found in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections.
rows.anchor: فإنه عارضه به عامئذ مرتين؛ ولهذا قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لفاطمة ابنته

rows.speaker: محمد بن سيرين
rows.claim: Ibn Sirin reports that after the Prophet’s death Ali vowed to collect the Qur’an in a codex before wearing his robe again, then explained to Abu Bakr that his vow was not opposition to the caliphate and gave allegiance.
rows.anchor: عن محمد بن سيرين قال: لما توفي النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أقسم علي ألا يرتدي برداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir notes the Ali report is disconnected; only the weak narrator Ashʿath mentions a codex, while other transmitters’ wording means Ali completed memorizing the Qur’an, since a memorizer is called one who collected it.
rows.anchor: هكذا رواه وفيه انقطاع، ثم قال: لم يذكر المصحف أحد إلا أشعث (10) وهو لين الحديث (11)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says he learned that فاطر means ‘initiated’ when a Bedouin described beginning a well; Ibn Kathir grades the chain good.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، عن ابن عباس، قال: كنت لا أدري ما {فاطر السماوات والأرض} [فاطر: 1] ، حتى أتاني أعرابيان

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر بن جرير الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari argues that the Qur’an descended in some Arab tongues, not all, since Arab tongues and dialects number more than seven and cannot be counted.
rows.anchor: قال الإمام أبو جعفر بن جرير الطبري، رحمه الله، بعد ما أورد طرفا مما تقدم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion asks what evidence supports the dialect account of the seven letters over the alternate view that they mean commands, prohibitions, exhortation, warnings, stories, and parables.
rows.anchor: وما برهانك على ما قلته دون أن يكون معناه ما قاله مخالفوك، من أنه نزل بأمر وزجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says advocates of the thematic explanation do not claim that it is the meaning of the earlier reports about seven letters; they mean the Qur’an came in seven aspects, as transmitted from the Prophet and Companions.
rows.anchor: إن الذين قالوا ذلك لم يدعوا أن تأويل الأخبار التي تقدم ذكرها، هو ما زعمت

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب وعبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Reports from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn Masʿud say the Qur’an descended from seven gates of Paradise.
rows.anchor: في رواية عن أبي بن كعب وعبد الله بن مسعود: أن القرآن نزل من سبعة أبواب الجنة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر بن جرير الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari explains the seven gates as the Qur’an’s meanings—commands, prohibitions, encouragement, warning, stories, and parables—which lead those who practice them to Paradise.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جرير: والأبواب السبعة من الجنة هي المعاني التي فيها من الأمر والنهي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas answers that the Prophet left only what is between the two covers; Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya gives the same answer. Al-Bukhari alone transmits this report.
rows.anchor: على ابن عباس، فقال له شداد بن معقل: أترك النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم من شيء؟ قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir explains that the report means the Prophet left no inheritable property, supporting it with Amr ibn al-Harith’s statement that he left no money, enslaved person, or other property.
rows.anchor: ومعناه: أنه، عليه السلام، ما ترك مالا ولا شيئا يورث عنه، كما قال عمرو بن الحارث

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Abu al-Darda reports the teaching that prophets leave no dinar or dirham as inheritance; they leave knowledge, and whoever takes it receives an abundant share.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أبي الدرداء: " إن الأنبياء لم يورثوا دينارا ولا درهما، وإنما ورثوا العلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas means by ‘what is between the covers’ the Qur’an; the Sunnah explains and clarifies it, while God’s Book is the primary inheritance. Ibn Kathir links this to 35:32.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال ابن عباس: وإنما ترك ما بين الدفتين يعني: القرآن، والسنة مفسرة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says the prophets were created to call people toward the Hereafter, not to accumulate worldly goods and pass them on.
rows.anchor: فالأنبياء، عليهم السلام، لم يخلقوا للدنيا يجمعونها ويورثونها، إنما خلقوا للآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet states, ‘We are not inherited; what we leave is charity,’ establishing the rule Ibn Kathir discusses.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: " لا نورث ما تركنا فهو صدقة

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr first publicly affirmed this teaching when asked about the Prophet’s inheritance; Ibn Kathir says many Companions accepted his transmission, including Umar, Uthman, Ali, Abbas, Talha, al-Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Abu Hurayra, and Aisha.
rows.anchor: وكان أول من أظهر هذه المحاسن من هذا الوجه أبو بكر الصديق، رضي الله عنه، لما سئل

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that God kept sending revelation to the Messenger, with its greatest frequency, until shortly before his death.
rows.anchor: أخبرني أنس بن مالك أن الله تابع الوحي على رسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم قبل وفاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir explains that revelation came gradually whenever needed; after the initial pause following the angel’s first descent, it did not lapse again and then came in a steady succession.
rows.anchor: ومعناه: أن الله تعالى تابع نزول الوحي على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم شيئا بعد شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first revelation was the command ‘Read in the name of your Lord’; the following hiatus lasted about two years or more, and the first revelation after it was the command to rise and warn.
rows.anchor: بعد نزول الملك أول مرة بقوله: {اقرأ باسم ربك} [العلق: 1] فإنه استلبث الوحي بعدها حينا يقال: قريبا من سنتين

rows.speaker: جندب بن عبد الله البجلي
rows.claim: Jundab reports that after the Prophet was ill for a night or two, a woman said his Satan had abandoned him, and Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā was revealed in response; Ibn Kathir notes its transmission by al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasaʾi.
rows.anchor: سمعت جندبا يقول: اشتكى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فلم يقم ليلة أو ليلتين، فأتته امرأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir explains that these reports belong in a discussion of Qur’an’s virtues because they show God’s great care and love for the Messenger: revelation was not cut off, and the Qur’an came piecemeal as an honor to him.
rows.anchor: والمناسبة في ذكر هذا الحديث والذي قبله في فضائل القرآن: أن الله تعالى له برسوله عناية عظيمة

rows.speaker: القاضي الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani reports that his codex began with ‘Read in the name of your Lord, the Most Generous’; Ibn Masʿud’s began with al-Fatiha’s ‘Master of the Day of Judgment,’ while Ubayy’s began with al-Fatiha and then placed surahs in a different order.
rows.anchor: حكى القاضي الباقلاني: أن أول مصحفه كان: "اقرأ باسم ربك الأكرم" وأول مصحف ابن مسعود: {مالك يوم الدين}

rows.speaker: القاضي الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani considers it possible that Companions exercised judgment in arranging the surahs in today’s codex; Makki says the order of verses and the opening basmalas came from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: ثم قال القاضي: ويحتمل أن ترتيب السور في المصحف على ما هو عليه اليوم من اجتهاد الصحابة

rows.speaker: ربيعة
rows.claim: Asked why al-Baqara and Aal ʿImran lead despite more than eighty surahs preceding them in revelation, Rabiʿa answers that knowledgeable compilers arranged the Qur’an by consensus, so the matter is not open to questioning.
rows.anchor: سمعت سليمان بن بلال يقول: سئل ربيعة: لم قدمت البقرة وآل عمران، وقد نزل قبلهما

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says the Qur’an’s arrangement follows what the Companions heard from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وسمعت مالكا يقول: إنما ألف القرآن على ما كانوا يسمعونه من النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن بن بطال
rows.claim: Ibn Battal says surah order in the written codex is not binding in prayer, recitation, or study; he cites Aisha’s statement that whichever surah one reads first is harmless and the Prophet’s use of nonconsecutive surahs in successive prayer units.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الحسن بن بطال: إنا نجد (5) تأليف سوره في الرسم والخط خاصة ولا يعلم أن أحدا منهم قال

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Battal explains that Ibn Masʿud and Ibn Umar’s censure of reading the Qur’an backwards means reversing a surah from end to beginning; that practice is forbidden, not merely reading surahs out of codex order.
rows.anchor: وأما ما روي عن ابن مسعود وابن عمر أنهما كرها أن يقرأ القرآن منكوسا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud describes al-Israʾ, al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta Ha, and the Prophets as among the ancient early surahs and among his old, long-held possessions; al-Bukhari alone transmits this report.
rows.anchor: سمعت ابن مسعود يقول في بني إسرائيل والكهف ومريم وطه والأنبياء: إنهن من العتاق الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir glosses ‘the ancient ones’ as early revelation and ‘my talad’ as old possessions or memorized material; talid means old wealth or goods, contrasted with tarif, the new.
rows.anchor: والمراد منه ذكر ترتيب هذه السور في مصحف ابن مسعود كالمصاحف العثمانية، وقوله: "من العتاق الأول" أي: من قديم ما نزل
